content: An aerobic organism, also known as an aerobe, is an organism that relies on oxygen for its metabolic processes. These organisms utilize oxygen in a process called cellular respiration, where substrates such as sugars and fats are oxidized to generate energy. Obligate aerobes are organisms that strictly require oxygen to carry out aerobic cellular respiration. In contrast, facultative anaerobes are capable of using oxygen when it is available but can also switch to anaerobic methods of energy production in its absence. Microaerophiles are organisms that can utilize oxygen but only at low concentrations, as higher levels may be harmful to them. Aerotolerant organisms, while able to survive in the presence of oxygen, do not use it as a terminal electron acceptor and are therefore considered anaerobic. A classic example of aerobic respiration is the oxidation of glucose, a monosaccharide. This process releases approximately 2880 kJ of energy per mole of glucose, which is conserved in the regeneration of 38 molecules of ATP from 38 molecules of ADP. This energy yield is about 19 times greater than that of typical anaerobic reactions. However, in eukaryotic organisms, which include all organisms except bacteria, the net gain is slightly lower at 36 ATP molecules per glucose molecule. This reduction is due to the need for active transport across an additional membrane. During the oxidation of glucose, oxygen is consumed, and water is produced as a byproduct. This overall process is a summary of three interconnected biochemical pathways: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle (also known as the citric acid cycle), and oxidative phosphorylation. Most animals, many fungi, and several bacteria are obligate aerobes, meaning they depend entirely on oxygen for survival. In contrast, most anaerobic organisms are bacteria. While being an obligate aerobe provides a significant energetic advantage, it also exposes the organism to high levels of oxidative stress, which can be damaging. Yeast serves as an example of a facultative aerobe, as it can switch between aerobic and anaerobic metabolism depending on oxygen availability. Similarly, individual human cells are facultative aerobes; they can perform lactic acid fermentation in the absence of oxygen. However, this anaerobic state cannot be sustained for long periods at the level of the entire organism, making humans obligate aerobes. Examples of obligate aerobic bacteria include Nocardia (Gram-positive), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Gram-negative), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast), and Bacillus species (Gram-positive).
